title: Night Shift
teaser: Every night at 3 a.m., the same caller asks for Karim by name. The system says he doesn’t exist.
paragraphs: At 2:55 a.m., the call centre in Smart Village is half asleep. Forty people in headsets answer calls from Britain, where it is still evening. Karim, thirty-one, has done this job for four years. He knows the script by heart: Thank you for calling Northline, my name is Karim, how can I help you today?

He is good at it, mostly. His English is clear, his manager says, but “too careful”. When customers speak fast or get angry, Karim freezes for a second, and that second feels like an hour. Next month, the company will choose a new team leader. Everyone says it will be Karim or Dalia. Dalia never freezes.

At exactly 3:00 a.m., his line lights up. “Good evening,” says an old man’s voice, slow and polite. “Am I speaking to Karim?” Karim blinks. Customers never ask for him by name; calls are random. “Yes, sir. How can I help you today?”

“My name is Arthur Harris. I have a question about my internet bill.” The question is simple, and Karim fixes it in two minutes. But Mr Harris doesn’t hang up. “You sound tired, young man. Do you like this job?” The script has no answer for that. Karim laughs nervously. “It’s… a good job, sir.” “That isn’t what I asked,” Mr Harris says kindly, and ends the call.

The next night, at 3:00 a.m. exactly, the line lights up again. And the night after that. Each time, the question is easy, and each time, Mr Harris asks one personal question at the end: about Karim’s family, his dreams, the first English word he ever learned. Strangely, Karim starts to look forward to 3 a.m. With Mr Harris, he never freezes.

On the fifth night, Dalia leans over his desk. “Who do you keep talking to? The system says those calls come from a number that doesn’t exist.” Karim checks his screen. She is right. The caller ID is just a line of zeros.

At 3:00 a.m., the phone lights up. “Karim,” says Mr Harris, and this time his voice is serious. “I know about the job offer in Dubai. Please listen to me carefully. Don’t take it.” Karim stops breathing. He hasn’t told anyone about Dubai. Not his manager, not Dalia. Not even his mother.

title: Night Shift
teaser: Karim asks IT to trace the calls. What they find makes no sense.
previously: Every night at 3 a.m., a polite old man called Arthur Harris calls Karim at the call centre. The caller ID is a line of zeros. Last night, Harris told him not to take a job in Dubai that nobody knows about.

openings.A: When the shift ends, Karim tells Dalia everything. She listens with her arms crossed, then laughs. “It’s Hossam from IT. He loves pranks. He probably read your messages.” But when they ask Hossam, he looks genuinely confused.
openings.B: Karim says nothing to Dalia, but he can feel her watching him for the rest of the shift. At 7 a.m., he goes alone to the IT office, where Hossam, his friend from university, is finishing his coffee.

paragraphs: Hossam types quickly and frowns at his screen. “That’s weird. Every call in this building is recorded and logged: time, number, length. Your calls at three o’clock are logged, so they really happened. But the number is zeros, and there’s no recording. It’s like the system received them from inside.”
“From inside the building?” Karim asks. Hossam shrugs. “Or from someone who knows our system very well. Either way, it isn’t a normal customer.”

On the bus home, Karim looks at the message from his cousin Amr. Two weeks ago, Amr wrote: “Hotel in Dubai needs a guest relations officer. Double your salary. I told them about you. They want an answer by the end of the month.” Karim hasn’t answered yet. Double the salary would mean a flat of his own, help for his parents, maybe even marriage one day.
That night, at 3:00 a.m., the line lights up. Karim answers before the first ring ends. “Who are you, Mr Harris? How do you know about Dubai?”

There is a soft laugh. “Those are good questions, but they’re not the most important ones. Before you accept any job, Karim, you should ask three questions. What exactly are the hours? Where will you live? And what happens to your visa if you want to leave? Ask your cousin. Write down the answers, not what you hope the answers are.”
Karim writes the three questions on a sticky note. Then he says, “I want to understand. Could you clarify what you mean by…” But the old man interrupts him gently.

“Tomorrow, I won’t call,” he says. “Someone else will. When she does, don’t freeze. Repeat her words, slow down, and breathe. Goodnight, Karim.” The line goes dead, and the screen shows nothing at all, not even the zeros.

to record something in an official system

title: Night Shift
teaser: An angry customer, a manager listening in, and five seconds of silence.
previously: The 3 a.m. calls are logged but have no number. Karim’s cousin offered him a job in Dubai. Mr Harris gave him three questions to ask, then said: tomorrow someone else will call. Don’t freeze.
paragraphs: The next night, the manager, Ms Rasha, sits at the end of Karim’s row with a headset and a notebook. “Team leader assessments,” she announces. “I’ll be listening to some of your calls this week. Just be yourselves.” Nobody is reassured.

At 3:00 a.m., Karim’s line lights up. The caller ID is a normal British number. Before he can finish the script, a woman starts shouting. “This is the third time I’m calling! My internet has been down for four days, I work from home, and every time I call, someone promises to fix it and nobody does anything!”

Karim feels the familiar freeze. His mind goes blank, and the silence grows: one second, two, three. Out of the corner of his eye, he sees Ms Rasha writing something. Dalia, at the next desk, glances at him.

Then he hears Mr Harris’s voice in his memory: repeat her words, slow down, breathe. Karim takes a breath. “Mrs Clarke, I completely understand why you’re upset. Your internet has been down for four days, you work from home, and you’ve called three times without a solution. That isn’t acceptable, and I’m sorry.”
The shouting stops. There is a surprised silence on the line. “Well… yes. Exactly,” she says, much more quietly.

Karim checks her account carefully. The previous agents opened three separate tickets, and nobody connected them, so the engineers never saw the full problem. He merges the tickets, marks the case as urgent and books an engineer for the next morning. Then he gives Mrs Clarke his own reference number. “If anything goes wrong, use this number and ask for me.”

When the call ends, Ms Rasha takes off her headset and looks at him for a long moment. She doesn’t say anything, but she underlines something twice in her notebook. After the shift, as Karim waits for the bus, his personal phone buzzes. A voicemail. No number. He presses play, and hears a familiar, slow voice: “Well done, Karim. Now call your cousin and ask the three questions.”

title: Night Shift
teaser: Double the salary. But the answers to the three questions are not what Amr promised.
previously: Karim calmed an angry customer while the manager was listening, and he didn’t freeze. Then a voicemail from Mr Harris told him to call his cousin in Dubai and ask the three questions.
paragraphs: Karim calls Amr on Saturday afternoon. In the background, he can hear traffic and Arabic music. “Finally!” Amr shouts. “So you’re coming? I told the manager you’re the best.”

Karim looks at his sticky note. “First, a few questions. What exactly are the hours?” Amr hesitates. “Normal hotel hours. Twelve hours a day, six days a week. But the tips are amazing, bro.” Karim writes it down. Seventy-two hours a week. His night shifts suddenly look short.

“Where will I live?” “Staff accommodation. It’s fine. A room with five other guys, but it’s close to the hotel.” Karim writes it down. “And if I want to leave before the contract ends, what happens to my visa?” This time, the silence is longer. “I… don’t know exactly. I think they keep your passport for the first year. Everybody does it.”

After the call, Karim reads his notes several times. The salary is double, but if he divides it by the hours, it is almost the same as now. A shared room with five strangers. A passport he can’t touch. Amr isn’t lying; he just doesn’t ask questions. He never has.

At the same time, Karim can’t ignore the other side. His father’s pension is small, and his sister’s wedding is next year. Staying in Smart Village means waiting for a promotion that might go to Dalia.

That night, Karim arrives early for his shift. Dalia is already there, eating a sandwich at her desk. She looks tired. “Rasha announced the final interviews,” she says. “Next Thursday. You and me.” She tries to smile. “May the best one win.”

At 3:00 a.m., there is no call from Mr Harris. Only the hum of the computers and the sound of forty people answering the evening of another country. Karim takes out his phone. Amr has sent a message: “The hotel needs an answer by Wednesday. Yes or no?”

title: Night Shift
teaser: In the waiting room, Dalia tells Karim why she needs this job.
previously: Karim learned the truth about the Dubai job: 72-hour weeks, a shared room and a passport kept by the hotel. The team leader interviews are on Thursday: Karim against Dalia.

openings.A: Karim sends Amr one word: “Yes.” Then he feels sick for two days. He tells himself it is the sensible choice, but every night at 3 a.m. he looks at the phone, hoping it will light up.
openings.B: Karim writes to Amr: “Not yet. I need to wait for a decision here.” Amr sends back an angry face and “Your loss, bro.” Karim feels strangely calm, as if he has put down something heavy.

paragraphs: On Thursday, the final interviews take place in a small glass room on the second floor. Karim and Dalia sit outside on plastic chairs, both in their best shirts, both pretending to read something on their phones.

After ten minutes of silence, Dalia puts her phone down. “Can I tell you something?” she says quietly. “My mother is sick. Kidney problems. The treatment is expensive, and my salary isn’t enough. If I don’t get this job, I don’t know what I’ll do.”

Karim doesn’t know what to say. In four years, Dalia has never talked about her family. At work, she is fast, confident and a little cold. Now she looks younger and very tired. “I’m sorry,” he says, and he means it.
“I’m not telling you so you’ll lose on purpose,” she adds quickly. “I just… needed to say it to someone.”
Dalia goes in first. Through the glass, Karim can see her talking with her hands, the way she does when she is passionate. Forty minutes later, she comes out, gives him a small nod and walks away.

Karim’s interview starts with a role-play. Ms Rasha pretends to be an agent who keeps freezing on calls. “How would you help me?” she asks. Karim smiles a little. He tells her about repeating the customer’s words, slowing down and breathing, and about connecting tickets instead of opening new ones. He doesn’t mention Mr Harris.

At the end, Ms Rasha closes her notebook. “Thank you, Karim. We’ve almost made our decision.” She pauses and studies his face. “But before we tell you, I need to ask you something. Who is Arthur Harris?”

title: Night Shift
teaser: The truth about the 3 a.m. caller is stranger, and kinder, than Karim imagined.
previously: After Karim’s team leader interview, Ms Rasha asked him a question he didn’t expect: who is Arthur Harris?
paragraphs: Karim’s mouth goes dry. “He’s… a customer,” he says. “He calls at three o’clock.” Ms Rasha almost smiles. She turns her laptop towards him. On the screen is a staff profile with a photo of a white-haired man with kind eyes. Arthur Harris. Senior Communication Coach. Retired.

“Arthur worked for Northline in Manchester for thirty years,” Ms Rasha explains. “He trained hundreds of agents. When he retired, he offered to help our centre for free. He calls a few promising agents through our internal training line. That’s why the number shows as zeros.”

Karim stares at the photo. “So the calls were… a test?” “Not a test,” she says. “Coaching. He believes people learn better from conversations than from courses. He doesn’t tell anyone who he is, because people perform when they know they are being trained. He wanted to hear the real you.”

“But Dubai,” Karim says. “Nobody knew about Dubai.” This time, Ms Rasha laughs out loud. “Your cousin Amr knew. He posted on Facebook: ‘My cousin Karim is joining me in Dubai soon!’ and he tagged you. Arthur reads everything about the people he coaches. He’s very thorough.”
Karim covers his face with his hands, half embarrassed and half relieved. He isn’t crazy. There is no ghost in the system, just an old man in Manchester who decided to care.

“Arthur sent me his notes about you,” Ms Rasha continues. “He wrote: ‘Karim doesn’t lack English. He lacks belief. When he stops trying to be perfect, he is the calmest agent I have ever heard.’” She closes the laptop.
“So,” says Karim carefully, “does that mean the job is mine?” Ms Rasha’s face becomes serious again. “Not yet,” she says. “You see, Dalia had calls from a coach too. Her name was Margaret.”

title: Night Shift
teaser: On the roof at sunrise, two rivals compare notes. Then Karim makes a decision.
previously: Arthur Harris turned out to be a retired coach who secretly coached promising agents. The team leader job isn’t decided yet: Dalia was coached too, by a woman called Margaret.
paragraphs: After the shift, Karim finds Dalia, his rival for the job, on the roof of the building, where some agents go to watch the sunrise before going home. The sky over Smart Village is turning orange. She hands him a cup of tea without asking.

“Margaret?” he says. Dalia laughs, a real laugh this time. “Every night at 4:30. She asked me terrible questions. ‘Why are you always in a hurry, dear?’ ‘What would happen if you made one mistake?’ I thought she was a crazy old lady with too much free time.”

“Harris asked me if I liked my job,” Karim says. “I didn’t know the answer.” Dalia looks at him. “And now?” Karim thinks about it honestly. “I like the moment when a person is shouting, and then they calm down because someone finally listened. I don’t love the script. I love that moment.”

Dalia nods slowly. “I like fixing things fast. I like numbers, targets, the board with everyone’s results. Margaret said I would be a good team leader if I learned to slow down sometimes.” She sips her tea. “She said you would be a good coach.”

They are quiet for a while, watching the sun. Karim thinks about the yellow numbers on the results board, about Dalia’s mother, about seventy-two-hour weeks in Dubai and a passport in a hotel drawer. He realises that he has been asking the wrong question. Not “How do I win?” but “What do I actually want to do every day?”

“Dalia,” he says. “If I told Rasha that I think you should be team leader, would that be strange?” Dalia stares at him. “Very strange. And very stupid, if you want the money.” She pauses. “Why would you do that?”
Karim smiles. He isn’t completely sure yet. He has an idea, a risky one, and he needs to say it to Ms Rasha before he changes his mind.

phrase.en: I don’t love the script. I love the moment when someone finally feels heard.

title: Night Shift
teaser: The last 3 a.m. call of the season. This time, Karim is on the other end.
previously: On the roof, Karim realised he loves calming people more than winning. He went to tell Ms Rasha his decision about the team leader job.

openings.A: “Dalia should be team leader,” Karim tells Ms Rasha. “She’s faster than me, and she loves the numbers. But I have another idea. New agents freeze, like I did. What if someone coached them, the way Arthur coached me?” Ms Rasha leans back in her chair and, for the first time, smiles widely.
openings.B: “I still want the team leader job,” Karim tells Ms Rasha. “Let the best one win.” She nods. “Fair. But let me tell you what Arthur recommended.” She reads from his notes: a new role, coaching new agents who freeze. “He thinks that’s where you belong. Think about it.” Karim thinks about it for ten seconds. Then he says yes.

paragraphs: Two weeks later, the results board has a new name at the top: Dalia, Team Leader. Under it, there is a new line that never existed before: Karim, Quality and Confidence Coach. The salary is not double, but it is twenty percent higher, with day shifts twice a week.

Karim writes to Amr: “I’m staying. Thank you for thinking of me.” Amr replies with a long voice note. He complains about the heat, the hours and his roommates, and at the end he asks quietly, “Do you think Northline needs people in Dubai?” Karim laughs and promises to ask.
Dalia is a good team leader. She is still fast, but now, sometimes, she stops and asks, “Why are you in a hurry, dear?” Everyone knows where that comes from. Her mother’s treatment has started.
On Karim’s last night shift, at 3:00 a.m., his line lights up. Zeros. He smiles before he answers. “Good evening, Mr Harris.”

“Good evening, Coach,” says the slow voice. “I wanted to say goodbye. Margaret and I are going on holiday. Cornwall. She insists.” Karim laughs. “Arthur, why did you choose me?” There is a pause. “Because you were kind to customers even when you were afraid. Kind and afraid is a good place to start. Fear passes. Kindness stays.”

The next week, Karim sits next to his first new agent, a young woman from Minya named Shahd. Her first angry customer starts shouting, and Karim sees it on her face: the freeze, the blank mind, the silence growing.
He leans towards her and whispers, very slowly, “Repeat her words. Slow down. Breathe.” Shahd takes a breath, and begins.
